{{Short description|Non-linear regression method}}
{{Orphan|date=October 2025}}

'''Beta regression''' is a form of regression which is used when the [[response variable]], <math>y</math>, takes values within <math>(0, 1)</math> and can be assumed to follow a [[beta distribution]].<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |last=Cribari-Neto |first=Francisco |last2=Zeileis |first2=Achim |date=2010 |title=Beta Regression in R |url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/vignettes/betareg.html |website=cran.r-project.org}}</ref> It is generalisable to variables which takes values in the arbitrary open interval <math>(a, b)</math> through transformations.<ref name="auto1"/> Beta regression was developed in the early 2000s by two sets of statisticians: Kieschnick and McCullough in 2003 and Ferrari and Cribari-Neto in 2004.<ref name="auto2" />

== Description ==
{{One source section
| date = November 2025
}}
The modern beta regression process is based on the [[Beta distribution#Mean and sample size|mean/precision parameterisation of the beta distribution]]. Here the variable is assumed to be distributed according to <math>B(\mu, \phi)</math> where <math>\mu</math> is the [[mean]] and <math>\phi</math> is the precision. As the mean of the distribution, <math>\mu</math> is constrained to fall within <math>(0, 1)</math> but <math>\phi</math> is not. For given values of <math>\mu</math>, higher values of <math>\phi</math> result in a beta with a lower variance, hence its description as a precision parameter.<ref name="auto1" />

Beta regression has three major motivations. Firstly, beta-distributed variables are usually [[heteroscedastic]] of a form where the scatter is greater closer to the mean value and lesser in the tails, whereas [[linear regression]] assumes [[Homoscedasticity and heteroscedasticity|homoscedasticity]].<ref name="auto1" /> Secondly, while transformations are available to consider beta distributed dependent variables within the [[Generalized linear model|generalised linear regression]] frameworks, these transformation mean that the regressions model <math>y'</math> rather than <math>y</math>, so the interpretation is in terms of the mean of <math>y'</math> rather than the mean of <math>y</math>, which presents a more awkward interpretation.<ref name="auto1" /> Thirdly, values within <math>(0, 1)</math> are generally from [[skewed distribution]]s.<ref name="auto1" />

The basic algebra of the beta regression is linear in terms of the [[link function]], but even in the equal dispersion case presented below, it is not a special case of generalised linear regression:

<math display="block">g(\mu_i) = x_i^T\beta_i = \eta_i,</math>

where <math>g</math> is a link function.<ref name="auto1" />

It is also notable that the variance of <math>y</math> is dependent on <math>\mu</math> in the model, so beta regressions are naturally heteroscedastic.<ref name="auto1" />

== Variable dispersion beta regression ==
There is also variable dispersion beta regression, where <math>\phi</math> is modelled independently for each observation rather than being held constant.{{Explain|date=March 2023|reason=how exactly does one model phi?}} [[Likelihood-ratio test|Likelihood ratio tests]] can be "interpreted as testing the null hypothesis of equidispersion against a specific alternative of variable dispersion"<ref name="auto1" /> by using normal versus variable dispersions. For example, within the [[R (programming language)|R programming language]], the formula "<math>y \sim x_1 + x_2</math>" describes an equidispersion model but it might be compared to any of the following three specific variable dispersion alternatives:

* <math>y\sim x_1 + x_2 | z_1</math>
* <math>y\sim x_1 + x_2 | z_2</math>
* <math>y\sim x_1 + x_2 | z_1 + z_2</math>

The choice of link equation can render the need for variable dispersion irrelevant, at least when judged in terms of model fit.<ref name="auto1"/>

A quasi [[Ramsey RESET test|RESET diagnostic test]] (inspired by RESET, i.e. regression specification error test) is available for considering misspecification, particularly in the context of link equation choice.<ref name="auto1"/> If a power of a fitted mean/linear predictor is used as a covariate and it results in a better model than the same formula without the power term, then the original model formula is a misspecification. This quasi-RESET diagnostic procedure may also be considered graphically, for example by comparing the absolute raw residuals for each model as the <math>(x, y)</math> values, with the model that has the smaller absolute residual more often is to be preferred.<ref name="auto1"/>

In general, the closer the observed <math>y</math> values are to the <math>(a, b)</math> extremes, the more significant the choice of link function.<ref name="auto1"/>

The link function can also affect whether the [[Maximum likelihood estimation|MLE]] procedure statistical programs use to implement beta regressions converge. Furthermore the MLE procedure can tend to underestimate the standard errors and therefore significance inferences in beta regression.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |last=Grün |first=Bettina |last2=Kosmidis |first2=Ioannis |last3=Zeileis |first3=Achim |date=2012 |title=Extended Beta Regression in R: Shaken, Stirred, Mixed, and Partitioned |url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/vignettes/betareg-ext.html |website=cran.r-project.org}}</ref> In practice, however, Bias Correction (BC) and Bias Reduction (BR) are essentially diagnostic steps, i.e. the analyst compares the model with neither BC nor BR to two models, each implementing one of BC and BR.<ref name="auto"/>

The assumptions of beta regression are:

* link appropriateness ("deviance residuals vs. indices of observation", at least for the logit link<ref name="auto2">{{Cite journal|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.3940|title=A case for beta regression in the natural sciences|first1=Emilie A.|last1=Geissinger|first2=Celyn L. L.|last2=Khoo|first3=Isabella C.|last3=Richmond|first4=Sally J. M.|last4=Faulkner|first5=David C.|last5=Schneider|date=February 20, 2022|journal=Ecosphere|volume=13|issue=2|doi=10.1002/ecs2.3940|s2cid=247101790 |url-access=subscription|doi-access=free}}</ref>)
* homogenous residuals ("deviance residuals vs. linear predictor"<ref name="auto2"/>)
* [[Normal distribution|normality]] ("half-normal plot of deviance residuals"<ref name="auto2"/>)
* no outliers ("[[Cook's distance]] to determine outliers"<ref name="auto2"/>)
